records.name: Occitanie
records.summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident record survives in this region's sources; that absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not as evidence of local safety. The national framework documented in this record applies unchanged in every commune and department.

That framework is centred on custody. Under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a prisoner is placed by the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still legally marked male are held in all-male facilities; a January 2018 investigation records one such detainee three days in a men's facility near Lille amid inmate threats, and another held in notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial in the capital. The national detention inspector-general's May 2021 opinion — covering every place of deprivation of liberty, built on some forty referrals since 2010 — finds serious violations persisting: isolation for trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never written into prison rules; it recommends that detainees choose the sex of search officers and ward, prohibits identity-based isolation, and requires continuity of medical care, and names transgender detainees as the group that suffers most in the state's custody.

records.name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
records.summary: Region research direction: mixed — the country's largest LGBTQ+ community and its biggest police raids coexist, with police acting without legal basis. (1) 1 February 2025: police arrested 56 men at a hotel in the capital at a reported "gay sex party"; organisers risk pornography-law prosecution with penalties up to 15 years; Amnesty International Indonesia called the police's "discriminatory and senseless harassment of LGBTI people ... has no basis in law" and demanded release of those detained. (2) One of the eight provinces where an international NGO found discriminatory regional regulations — and simultaneously the city with the country's densest LGBTQ+ infrastructure, media presence and monitoring-group offices; an assessor should expect both to be true at once. National climate from this record's sources: an October 2025 presidential decree listed "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among the country's non-military national security threats alongside terrorism and drugs, amplifying self-censorship (editors killing LGBTQ+ stories for fear of state reprisal); police deny violence and extortions in the 2022 death-in-custody of a US-based trans activist arrested on drug charges at Bali airport while family members allege he was beaten. Model-estimate residual (route 3, best-knowledge delta): sheer scale of the community limits enforcement reach.

records.name: Mahārāshtra
records.summary: Region research direction: worse than national on public-festival access screening — religion-based identity verification doubles as an outing mechanism for gender-nonconforming visitors. After the VHP publicly urged garba (autumn dance festival) organisers not to allow non-Hindus and to check Aadhaar cards for entry, a political row erupted; in Nagpur organisers imposed Aadhaar verification, security checks with "male and female" boundaries and a ritual bow before a Varaha avatar as entry conditions. An identity-checked, religion-screened entry gate at a public festival is precisely the mechanism by which a gender-nonconforming visitor is examined and outed by authorities who are not supposed to be involved — and it is happening in named cities, not nationwide. National backdrop from this record's sources: parliament passed a 2026 amendment bill removing the right to self-identify, limiting recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification for gender-affirming procedures, and creating offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender punishable with up to life in prison — prompting nationwide protests from trans communities, with a Supreme Court-appointed panel asking the government to withdraw it; the national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards needed for social security.

records.name: Delhi
records.summary:
Delhi sits at the centre of the country's 2026 reversal on trans rights: parliament passed an amendment bill removing the right to self-identification, restricting legal recognition to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification, and creating new offences of coercion and allurement punishable up to life imprisonment — a de facto reversal of the 2014 constitutional self-determination ruling, cleared by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. The bill triggered rallies in the capital in March 2026, and a supreme-court-appointed advisory panel urged its withdrawal amid privacy and dignity challenges.

The capital is also where the country's trans population is most institutionally visible: the most recent national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, of whom roughly 32,500 held identity documents — the documentation gap and the protest politics both concentrate here.

records.name: Seoul
records.summary:
The capital's courts have been the country's clearest rights forum for trans people: a ruling finalised in July 2024 held that police who told a transgender person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while had infringed personal rights, calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right and awarding damages. A 2021 national human-rights-commission survey (591 trans respondents) quantified the underlying fear: 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid public restrooms, 36% went without; a 2021 district-court judgment awarded damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

Recognition has also liberalised judicially: a May 2024 regional decision approved gender-marker change for five trans people without surgery, holding that a surgery requirement violates bodily integrity and reducing the old surgical prerequisites to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them.

records.name: Quintana Roo
records.summary: Quintana Roo: worse than national for what a visitor actually meets — the country's main tourist corridor, with a documented policing problem. The Cancún/Riviera Maya hotel zone is a massive international tourism envelope with a commercially gay-friendly surface, but municipal and state police have been repeatedly documented committing discriminatory acts against LGBT+ people, with multiple recorded assaults during detention concentrated in Tulum and Playa del Carmen; the community describes officers as untrained in human-rights standards. The municipal Directorate for Sexual Diversity recorded three formal discrimination complaints in a single year, including violence against a transgender woman, and two Tourist Police members were fired after their own body cameras showed them running an extortion ring against visitors with portable card terminals. Cancún's immigration detention facility is documented as a place of systematic rights violations with no accountability — relevant to a visitor whose documents are questioned. Countervailing: the state enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and banned conversion practices in December 2023. Scored relative to the national score (0.55) for Mexico.

records.name: Selangor
records.summary:
This state is where the country's religious-enforcement apparatus has been most visibly exercised against gender expression: in 2021 its religious department issued an arrest warrant for a prominent transgender businesswoman over her presentation and mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers in a manhunt that preceded her leaving the country, an episode documented in international analysis of state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

The national framework applies unchanged here: same-sex conduct is criminalised with sentences up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and the day-to-day exposure for gender-nonconforming visitors runs precisely through this state's religious-offence enforcement.

records.name: Johor
records.summary:
Johor operates within the national framework without documented local divergence: same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and public-morality offences are enforced through the state's religious authorities — the channel international monitoring documents as driving state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

No protective or tolerant regime specific to this state is on record. A visitor's exposure here is the national baseline, enforced locally.
